concept.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory
concept.concept_description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.

concept.lean_guess: Given an n-player game G with strategy sets S_1, ..., S_n. Define the simplex Delta = {(p_1, ..., p_n) : p_i in Delta(S_i), sum p_i = 1}. Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.

concept.title: Sheaf-Theoretic Data Integration: When Databases Form a Sheaf
concept.concept_description: A database with missing entries is a partial section of a sheaf. The sheaf condition (gluing) says that if two partial sections agree on their overlap, they can be glued into a global section. Conjecture: the probability that a random database with missing rate r satisfies the sheaf condition (i.e., can be consistently filled in) is P(sheaf) = (1-r)^{C(n,k)} where n is the number of columns, k is the number of rows, and C(n,k) is the number of overlapping constraints. This means: for a database with n columns and k rows, the probability of consistent imputation drops exponentially with the number of overlapping constraints. The sheaf imputation method: fill in missing values by finding the closest global section of the data sheaf. This is equivalent to solving a constrained optimization problem where the constraints are the sheaf condition on every overlapping pair of feature subsets. Conjecture: sheaf imputation outperforms mean imputation and KNN imputation when the missing rate r < 0.5 and the number of features n > 10, because the sheaf condition provides exponentially many consistency constraints that other methods ignore. Test: generate synthetic databases with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compare sheaf imputation with mean, KNN, and MICE. Impact: data imputation is a sheaf cohomology problem. The sheaf condition is the natural consistency constraint for databases.

concept.lean_guess: Define the data sheaf: for a database with n features and m observations, the base space is the poset P of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion). The sheaf F assigns to each feature subset S the set of complete observations on features S. The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S project out the features in S\T. The sheaf condition: for any cover {S_i} of S, the following is an equalizer: F(S) -> prod_i F(S_i) ==> prod_{i,j} F(S_i cap S_j). This means: a global section exists iff local sections agree on overlaps. P(sheaf) = P(all overlapping constraints are consistent) = prod_{overlaps} P(consistent | missing) = prod_{overlaps} (1-r)^2 = (1-r)^{2*C(n,2)} for pairwise overlaps. More precisely: there are C(n,2) overlapping pairs of features. Each pair requires consistency of the two partial sections. P(consistent pair) = (1-r)^2 (both features present) + r^2 * P(consistent by chance) + 2*r*(1-r) * P(consistent partial). For random data: P(consistent by chance) ~ 1/k where k is the number of values. So P(sheaf) ~ (1 - r + r/k)^{C(n,2)}. For n > 10 and r < 0.5: P(sheaf) > (1-r)^{C(n,2)} > 0 if r < 1 - C(n,2)^{-1/n}. Sheaf imputation: find the global section s that minimizes ||s - data||^2 subject to s in H^0(F). This is a constrained optimization problem. Test: generate synthetic data from a known distribution, introduce MCAR missing values, compare imputation methods.

# Uniform Bond-Dimension Scaling Cannot Create a Min-Cut Phase Transition

This file formalizes a finite cut-capacity model for tensor-network entanglement
and proves a rigorous *negative/control* result: on a fixed weighted directed
graph, multiplying every edge weight by a positive natural number `D` (uniform
bond-dimension scaling) leaves the set of minimum cuts unchanged. Hence no sharp
min-cut "phase transition" can be produced by uniform bond-dimension scaling
alone.

## Setup

* A finite vertex type `V`.
* A weighted directed graph `w : V → V → ℕ`.
* `cutCap w S` : the capacity of the cut `S` (edges leaving `S`).
* `scaleWeight D w` : uniform scaling of all weights by `D`.

## Main Results

* `cutCap_scale` : `cutCap (scaleWeight D w) S = D * cutCap w S`.
* `cutCap_scale_le_iff` : for `0 < D`, scaling preserves capacity comparisons.
* `isMinCut_scale_iff` : for `0 < D`, the min-cut property is invariant under scaling.
* `no_uniform_bond_dimension_threshold` : for positive `D1 D2`, the min-cut
  property under `D1`-scaling agrees with that under `D2`-scaling — no threshold.
* `cutCap_completeUnitWeight` : a closed form for the complete unit-weight graph.

The discussion of the physical motivation (tensor networks, emergent geometry)
is intentionally kept out of the Lean statements and lives in `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`.

import Mathlib

open Finset

namespace UniformBondScaling

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- Capacity of the cut `S`: the total weight of edges from `S` to its complement. -/
def cutCap (w : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  ∑ x ∈ S, ∑ y ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun y => y ∉ S), w x y

/-- Uniform scaling of all edge weights by a factor `D` (the bond dimension). -/
def scaleWeight (D : ℕ) (w : V → V → ℕ) : V → V → ℕ := fun x y => D * w x y

/-- Scaling all weights by `D` scales every cut capacity by `D`. -/
theorem cutCap_scale (D : ℕ) (w : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) :
    cutCap (scaleWeight D w) S = D * cutCap w S := by
  simp only [cutCap, scaleWeight, Finset.mul_sum]

/-- For a positive scaling factor, comparisons of cut capacities are preserved. -/
theorem cutCap_scale_le_iff {D : ℕ} (hD : 0 < D) (w : V → V → ℕ) (S T : Finset V) :
    cutCap (scaleWeight D w) S ≤ cutCap (scaleWeight D w) T ↔ cutCap w S ≤ cutCap w T := by
  rw [cutCap_scale, cutCap_scale, Nat.mul_le_mul_left_iff hD]

/-- `S` is a minimum cut for `w` if its capacity is minimal among all cuts. -/
def IsMinCut (w : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) : Prop :=
  ∀ T : Finset V, cutCap w S ≤ cutCap w T

/-- For a positive scaling factor, the minimum-cut property is invariant. -/
theorem isMinCut_scale_iff {D : ℕ} (hD : 0 < D) (w : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) :
    IsMinCut (scaleWeight D w) S ↔ IsMinCut w S := by
  unfold IsMinCut
  exact forall_congr' (fun T => cutCap_scale_le_iff hD w S T)

/-- **No uniform bond-dimension threshold.** For any two positive scaling factors,
the minimum-cut property under one scaling coincides with that under the other.
A fixed-topology, uniform-`D` model therefore admits no min-cut phase transition. -/
theorem no_uniform_bond_dimension_threshold {D1 D2 : ℕ} (h1 : 0 < D1) (h2 : 0 < D2)
    (w : V → V → ℕ) (S : Finset V) :
    IsMinCut (scaleWeight D1 w) S ↔ IsMinCut (scaleWeight D2 w) S := by
  rw [isMinCut_scale_iff h1, isMinCut_scale_iff h2]

/-- The complete graph with unit weights (no self loops). -/
def completeUnitWeight : V → V → ℕ := fun x y => if x = y then 0 else 1

/-- Closed form for the cut capacity of the complete unit-weight graph:
`|S| · (|V| - |S|)`, the number of ordered pairs crossing the cut. -/
theorem cutCap_completeUnitWeight (S : Finset V) :
    cutCap (completeUnitWeight (V := V)) S = S.card * (Fintype.card V - S.card) := by
  unfold cutCap completeUnitWeight
  have hfilt : (Finset.univ.filter (fun y => y ∉ S)) = Sᶜ := by
    ext y; simp [Finset.mem_compl]
  have hcard : (Finset.univ.filter (fun y => y ∉ S)).card = Fintype.card V - S.card := by
    rw [hfilt, Finset.card_compl]
  have hsum : ∀ x ∈ S, (∑ y ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun y => y ∉ S), if x = y then 0 else 1)
      = Fintype.card V - S.card := by
    intro x hx
    rw [← hcard]
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y hy => ?_), Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul, mul_one]
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter] at hy
    have : x ≠ y := by rintro rfl; exact hy.2 hx
    simp [this]
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hsum, Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul]

end UniformBondScaling

  * the Pesin / variational bridge between the Lyapunov exponent and entropy.

  1. `deriv_iterate_eq_prod`      — derivative of the n-th iterate is the orbit product (chain rule).
  2. `log_abs_deriv_iterate_eq_sum` — log of the stretching factor is a Birkhoff sum of `log|f'|`.

import Mathlib

open Filter Topology Finset

namespace LyapunovChaos

/-- Finite-time Lyapunov exponent of `f` at `x` over `n` steps: the average
exponential stretching rate of the derivative of the `n`-th iterate. The maximal
Lyapunov exponent of a chaotic system (such as the three-body problem) is the
`limsup` of this quantity; strict positivity is the hallmark of chaos. -/
def ftle (f : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  Real.log |deriv (f^[n]) x| / n

/-- Number of period-`n` points of the degree-`d` uniformly expanding circle map
`x ↦ d·x mod 1`. There are `dⁿ - 1` of them; their exponential growth rate is the
topological entropy of the map. -/
def periodicPointCount (d n : ℕ) : ℕ := d ^ n - 1

/-
!-- The derivative of the n-th iterate factors as a product along the orbit
by the chain rule (induction via `iterate_succ'` and `deriv_comp`). -- !--

**Chain rule for iterates.** The derivative of the `n`-th iterate of `f` at `x`
is the product of the derivatives of `f` taken along the forward orbit of `x`. This
is the multiplicative cocycle underlying every Lyapunov-exponent computation.
-/
theorem deriv_iterate_eq_prod (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    deriv (f^[n]) x = ∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, deriv f (f^[i] x) := by
  induction' n with n ih generalizing x;
  · norm_num;
  · convert deriv_comp _ ( hf _ ) ( show DifferentiableAt ℝ ( f^[n] ) x from ?_ ) using 1;
    · rw [ Function.iterate_succ' ];
    · rw [ Finset.prod_range_succ, ih, mul_comm ];

theorem log_abs_deriv_iterate_eq_sum (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f)

  rw [ ← Real.log_prod, deriv_iterate_eq_prod f hf ];
  · rw [ Finset.abs_prod ];

theorem abs_deriv_iterate_ge (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) {c : ℝ}

  · rw [ Finset.abs_prod ] ; exact le_trans ( by norm_num ) ( Finset.prod_le_prod ( fun _ _ => by positivity ) fun _ _ => hc _ ) ;

**Positivity of the maximal Lyapunov exponent ⇒ deterministic chaos.** For a

theorem ftle_ge_log (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) {c : ℝ} (hc : 1 < c)

/-! ## Character Tables -/

/-- A `CharacterTable` encodes the character theory of a finite group with `n`

structure CharacterTable (n : ℕ) where
  /-- Size of the j-th conjugacy class -/
  classSize : Fin n → ℕ
  /-- Order of the group -/
  groupOrder : ℕ
  /-- Character value: `χ i j` = value of the i-th irreducible character
      on elements of the j-th conjugacy class -/

  /-- The group order is positive -/
  groupOrder_pos : 0 < groupOrder
  /-- There is at least one conjugacy class -/
  n_pos : 0 < n
  /-- Every conjugacy class is nonempty -/
  classSize_pos : ∀ j, 0 < classSize j
  /-- The identity class (class 0) has size 1 -/

  trivial_char : ∀ j, χ ⟨0, n_pos⟩ j = 1
  /-- Class equation: ∑ |C_j| = |G| -/
  classEquation : ∑ j : Fin n, (classSize j : ℚ) = (groupOrder : ℚ)
  /-- Row orthogonality: ∑_k |C_k| χ_i(g_k) χ_j(g_k) = |G| δ_{i,j} -/
  rowOrth : ∀ i j : Fin n,
    ∑ k : Fin n, (classSize k : ℚ) * χ i k * χ j k =
      if i = j then (groupOrder : ℚ) else 0

  colOrth : ∀ k l : Fin n,

/-- A `MoonshineDatum` extends a character table with a graded module structure.

# Fractal Number Theory: Hausdorff and Box-Counting Dimensions of Prime Distributions

We study the set S = {1/log(p) : p prime} ⊂ ℝ, which is isometric to the primes
under the logarithmic metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|.

## Main Results

1. **dimH_logPrimeImage_eq_zero**: The Hausdorff dimension of S is 0.
2. **zero_mem_closure_logPrimeImage**: 0 is a limit point of S.
3. **logPrimeMetric_formula**: Explicit metric formula relating prime gaps to geometry.
4. **logPrimeImage_bounded**: S ⊆ (0, 1/log 2].
5. **logPrime_spacing_vanishes**: The gaps between consecutive 1/log(prime) values → 0.
6. **prime_dimension_gap**: dimH(S) = 0 yet 0 is a limit point (not isolated).

import Mathlib

open Real Set MeasureTheory Filter Topology ENNReal Nat

noncomputable section

/-! ## Core Definitions -/

/-- The logarithmic prime image: S = {1/log(p) : p is a prime natural number}. -/
def logPrimeImage : Set ℝ :=
  {x : ℝ | ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ x = 1 / Real.log p}

/-- The logarithmic prime metric on natural numbers:
d(p, q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. -/
def logPrimeMetricDist (p q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  |1 / Real.log p - 1 / Real.log q|

/-! ## Novel Definition: Box-Counting Dimension Framework

Box-counting (Minkowski) dimension for bounded subsets of ℝ.
This is distinct from Hausdorff dimension and can be positive for countable sets. -/

/-- The box-counting number N(S, ε): count of grid intervals of width ε intersecting S. -/
def boxCountingNumber (S : Set ℝ) (ε : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  if ε ≤ 0 then 0
  else (Finset.Icc (Int.floor (sInf S / ε)) (Int.ceil (sSup S / ε))).card

/-- The upper box-counting dimension:
dim_B^+(S) = limsup_{ε→0+} log(N(S,ε)) / log(1/ε). -/
def upperBoxDim (S : Set ℝ) : EReal :=
  Filter.limsup (fun ε => (Real.log (boxCountingNumber S ε : ℝ) / Real.log (1/ε) : EReal))
    (nhdsWithin (0 : ℝ) (Set.Ioi 0))

The prime gap energy in the logarithmic metric measures the "roughness" of
the prime distribution at a given scale exponent s. -/

/-- The prime gap energy at exponent s, summing |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|^s over
consecutive prime pairs up to bound N. This captures the fractal structure
at different scales: s=1 gives total variation, s < 1 emphasizes small gaps. -/
def primeLogGapEnergy (N : ℕ) (s : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ k ∈ Finset.range N,
    if (k.Prime ∧ (k+2).Prime) then
      |1 / Real.log (k : ℝ) - 1 / Real.log ((k+2 : ℕ) : ℝ)|^s
    else 0

/-- The logarithmic prime image is countable. -/
theorem logPrimeImage_countable : Set.Countable logPrimeImage :=
  Set.Countable.mono (fun x hx => by cases hx; aesop)

/-- **Main Theorem**: The Hausdorff dimension of the logarithmic prime image is 0.

theorem dimH_logPrimeImage_eq_zero : dimH logPrimeImage = 0 :=
  dimH_countable logPrimeImage_countable

/-- The logarithmic prime metric is symmetric. -/
theorem logPrimeMetric_symm (p q : ℕ) :
    logPrimeMetricDist p q = logPrimeMetricDist q p :=
  abs_sub_comm _ _

/-- The logarithmic prime metric satisfies the triangle inequality. -/
theorem logPrimeMetric_triangle (p q r : ℕ) :
    logPrimeMetricDist p r ≤ logPrimeMetricDist p q + logPrimeMetricDist q r := by
  convert abs_sub_le _ _ _ using 4; infer_instance

theorem logPrimeMetric_eq_zero_iff (p q : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (hq : q.Prime) :

  unfold logPrimeMetricDist
  norm_num [sub_eq_zero]
  exact ⟨fun h => Nat.cast_injective (Real.log_injOn_pos (by norm_num; exact hp.pos)
    (by norm_num; exact hq.pos) h), fun h => h ▸ rfl⟩

/-- For any prime p, 0 < 1/log(p). -/
theorem one_div_log_prime_pos (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    0 < 1 / Real.log p :=
  one_div_pos.mpr (Real.log_pos (Nat.one_lt_cast.mpr hp.one_lt))

theorem one_div_log_prime_le (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    1 / Real.log p ≤ 1 / Real.log 2 := by
  gcongr; norm_cast; exact hp.two_le

theorem logPrimeImage_bounded : logPrimeImage ⊆ Set.Ioc 0 (1 / Real.log 2) := by
  rintro x ⟨p, hp, rfl⟩; exact ⟨one_div_log_prime_pos p hp, one_div_log_prime_le p hp⟩

import Mathlib

/-!
# Hydrogen Atom: Dipole Transition Selection Rules

This file formalizes the electric dipole selection rules for the hydrogen atom:

- **Δm rule**: The magnetic quantum number must change by at most ±1
  for a nonzero dipole matrix element.

## Mathematical Context

The electric dipole operator for electromagnetic transitions has three
Cartesian components `x, y, z`. In spherical coordinates:
- `z = r cos θ` → involves `Y₁⁰(θ,φ)` ∝ `cos θ`
- `x = r sin θ cos φ` → involves `e^{iφ}` and `e^{-iφ}`
- `y = r sin θ sin φ` → involves `e^{iφ}` and `e^{-iφ}`

The azimuthal part of the matrix element `⟨ψ'|r̂_q|ψ⟩` contains
the integral `∫₀²π e^{-im'φ} f(φ) e^{imφ} dφ` where `f` is one of
`{1, e^{iφ}, e^{-iφ}}`. This integral vanishes unless `m' - m ∈ {0, ±1}`.

This file proves the selection rule from the orthogonality of complex
exponentials, which is the mathematical core of the selection rule.

## Key Results

* `dipole_m_selection_z`: Δm = 0 for z-polarized transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_plus`: Δm = +1 for σ⁺ transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_minus`: Δm = -1 for σ⁻ transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_vanishing`: matrix element vanishes when |Δm| > 1
-/

noncomputable section

open Complex Real MeasureTheory
open scoped BigOperators

/-! ## Dipole Matrix Element (Azimuthal Part)

The azimuthal part of the dipole matrix element for the three
polarization components `q ∈ {-1, 0, +1}` is:

  I_q(m', m) = ∫₀²π e^{-im'φ} e^{iqφ} e^{imφ} dφ
             = ∫₀²π e^{i(m - m' + q)φ} dφ

This equals `2π` if `m' = m + q` and `0` otherwise.
-/

/-- The azimuthal dipole integral for polarization `q` between
magnetic quantum numbers `m` and `m'`:
  `∫₀²π exp(i(m - m' + q)φ) dφ`
This is `2π` if `m + q = m'` and `0` otherwise. -/
def azimuthalDipoleIntegral (m m' q : ℤ) : ℂ :=
  ∫ φ in (0 : ℝ)..(2 * Real.pi),
    Complex.exp (↑((m - m' + q) * φ) * Complex.I)

/-
The azimuthal dipole integral equals `2π` when `m' = m + q`.
-/
theorem azimuthalDipoleIntegral_resonant (m q : ℤ) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m (m + q) q = ↑(2 * Real.pi) := by
  unfold azimuthalDipoleIntegral;
  simp

/-
The azimuthal dipole integral vanishes when `m' ≠ m + q`.
-/
theorem azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant
    (m m' q : ℤ) (h : m' ≠ m + q) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0 := by
  convert integral_exp_mul_complex ?_ using 1;
  convert intervalIntegral.integral_congr fun x _ => ?_ using 3;
  rotate_left;
  rotate_left;
  exact ↑ ( m - m' + q ) * Complex.I;
  · exact mul_ne_zero ( Int.cast_ne_zero.mpr ( by contrapose! h; linarith ) ) Complex.I_ne_zero;
  · push_cast; ring;
  · rw [ Complex.exp_eq_one_iff.mpr ⟨ m - m' + q, by push_cast; ring ⟩ ] ; norm_num

/-! ## Selection Rule for the z-Component (q = 0)

For z-polarized light, the azimuthal integral requires `m' = m`,
i.e., Δm = 0. -/

/-
**Δm = 0 selection rule**: For z-polarized dipole transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_z (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' 0 = 0 := by
  grind +suggestions

/-! ## Selection Rule for Circular Polarizations (q = ±1)

For right/left circularly polarized light, the azimuthal integral
requires `m' = m ± 1`, i.e., Δm = ±1. -/

/-
**Δm = +1 selection rule**: For σ⁺ transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m + 1`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_plus (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m + 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' 1 = 0 := by
  exact?

/-
**Δm = -1 selection rule**: For σ⁻ transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m - 1`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_minus (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m - 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' (-1) = 0 := by
  convert azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' ( -1 ) _ using 1;
  exact hne

/-! ## Combined Selection Rule -/

/-- **Full Δm selection rule**: The azimuthal dipole integral for
any spherical polarization component `q ∈ {-1, 0, 1}` vanishes
unless `m' = m + q`. This is the fundamental selection rule for
the magnetic quantum number. -/
theorem dipole_m_selection_general (m m' q : ℤ) (h : m' ≠ m + q) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0 :=
  azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' q h

/-- **Contrapositive form of the selection rule**: If the azimuthal
dipole matrix element is nonzero, then the change in `m` must be
exactly `q`, i.e., `Δm = q ∈ {-1, 0, +1}`. -/
theorem dipole_m_selection_contrapositive (m m' q : ℤ)
    (hne : azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q ≠ 0) :
    m' = m + q := by
  by_contra h
  exact hne (azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' q h)

/-
**Vanishing for forbidden transitions**: If `m' - m ∉ {-1, 0, 1}`,
then the azimuthal dipole integral vanishes for ALL polarization
components. This is the strong form of the selection rule.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_vanishing (m m' : ℤ)
    (hforbidden : ¬(m' - m = 0 ∨ m' - m = 1 ∨ m' - m = -1)) :
    (∀ q ∈ ({-1, 0, 1} : Set ℤ), azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0) := by
  -- Apply the off_resonant theorem to each case.
  intro q hq
  apply azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant;
  grind

/-! ## Selection Rule Completeness -/

/-
The allowed transitions are exactly those with `Δm ∈ {-1, 0, 1}`:
for each such value there exists a nonzero matrix element.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_complete (m : ℤ) (q : ℤ) (hq : q = -1 ∨ q = 0 ∨ q = 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m (m + q) q ≠ 0 := by
  exact azimuthalDipoleIntegral_resonant m q ▸ by norm_num [ Real.pi_ne_zero ] ;

end

# Topological Order, Genus Degeneracy, and Modular Data for Abelian Anyons

## Bridge: Finite Abelian Groups → Topological Quantum Field Theory → Quantum Memory

For an *abelian* anyon theory whose anyon labels form a finite abelian group `A` with
quantum dimension `d = |A|`, this file proves two complementary halves of the
anyon–TQFT dictionary:

1. **Ground-state degeneracy (GSD).** On a genus-`g` surface the ground space has
   dimension `GSD A g = d ^ g`.  We prove the per-handle recursion
   `GSD A (g+1) = d · GSD A g`, the connected-sum multiplicativity
   `GSD A (g+h) = GSD A g · GSD A h`, and the identification of `GSD A g` with the
   complex dimension of the free ground-state Hilbert space `(Fin g → A) →₀ ℂ`.

2. **Modular S-matrix.** From a nondegenerate braiding bicharacter we build the
   modular S-matrix `S_{a,b} = (1/√d) · χ_a(b)` and prove it is **unitary**,
   `∑_c S_{a,c} · conj S_{b,c} = δ_{a,b}`, via character orthogonality on `A`.

3. **A fully worked example.** For the cyclic anyon model `A = ZMod n` we *construct*
   an explicit `ModularBraiding (ZMod n)` from `ZMod.stdAddChar`, turning the
   conditional unitarity theorem into an unconditional statement and exhibiting the
   discrete Fourier matrix `S_{a,b} = (1/√n) exp(2πi a b / n)`.

This extends the catalog result `ToricCode.ground_space_dim` (which fixes the `ℤ/2`
toric code at the single value `4` on the torus) to *all* abelian anyon theories and
*all* genera, and supplies the previously missing braiding / modular-data half.
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset
open scoped ComplexConjugate

namespace TopologicalOrderGenus

/-! ## Section 1: Ground-State Degeneracy on Genus-`g` Surfaces

For an abelian theory the genus-`g` ground space is `A^{⊗g}`, so its dimension is
`|A|^g`.  We package this as `GSD` and prove its structural laws. -/

/-- Ground-state degeneracy of an abelian anyon theory `A` on a genus-`g` surface. -/
def GSD (A : Type*) [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : ℕ := Fintype.card A ^ g

variable {A : Type*}

-- !-- `GSD A g = d ^ g` by definition; the closed-form degeneracy law. -- !--
/-- **Closed form.** The genus-`g` degeneracy equals `d ^ g` with `d = |A|`. -/
theorem GSD_eq_pow [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : GSD A g = Fintype.card A ^ g := rfl

-- !-- Each added handle multiplies the degeneracy by `d = |A|`; this is `pow_succ`. -- !--
/-- **Per-handle recursion.** Adding one handle multiplies degeneracy by `d`. -/
theorem GSD_handle [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : GSD A (g + 1) = Fintype.card A * GSD A g := by
  rw [GSD, GSD, pow_succ, mul_comm]

-- !-- Genus is additive under connected sum, so degeneracy is multiplicative (`pow_add`). -- !--
/-- **Connected-sum multiplicativity.** `Σ_g # Σ_h` has degeneracy
    `GSD A g · GSD A h` since genus adds under connected sum. -/
theorem GSD_connected_sum [Fintype A] (g h : ℕ) :
    GSD A (g + h) = GSD A g * GSD A h := by
  rw [GSD, GSD, GSD, pow_add]

-- !-- The torus (`g = 1`) degeneracy is exactly `|A|`, the count of anyon types. -- !--
/-- **Torus.** On the torus the degeneracy is the number of anyon types. -/
theorem GSD_torus [Fintype A] : GSD A 1 = Fintype.card A := by
  rw [GSD, pow_one]

-- !-- The basis of the ground space is the set of flat configurations `Fin g → A`. -- !--
/-- **Combinatorial model.** `GSD A g` counts the configurations `Fin g → A`. -/
theorem GSD_eq_card_fun [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) :
    GSD A g = Fintype.card (Fin g → A) := by
  rw [GSD, Fintype.card_pi_const]

-- !-- The free ℂ-vector space on `Fin g → A` has finrank equal to its cardinality, `d^g`. -- !--
/-- **Hilbert-space dimension.** The free ground-state Hilbert space
    `(Fin g → A) →₀ ℂ` has complex dimension `GSD A g = d ^ g`. -/
theorem GSD_eq_finrank [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) :
    Module.finrank ℂ ((Fin g → A) →₀ ℂ) = GSD A g := by
  rw [Module.finrank_finsupp_self, GSD, Fintype.card_pi_const]

/-! ## Section 2: Modular Braiding and the Unitary S-matrix

A nondegenerate braiding on an abelian theory is a self-pairing of `A` by additive
characters, i.e. a group homomorphism `a ↦ χ_a` into `AddChar A ℂ` whose only element
pairing trivially with everything is `0`.  We encode this minimally. -/

/-- A **modular braiding** on a finite abelian group `A`: a family of additive
    characters `χ_a` depending homomorphically on `a` (`χ_{a+a'} = χ_a · χ_{a'}`) and
    *nondegenerate* (only `a = 0` gives the trivial character).  This is the abelian
    anyon braiding bicharacter `(a,b) ↦ χ_a(b)`. -/
structure ModularBraiding (A : Type*) [AddCommGroup A] [Fintype A] where
  /-- The braiding character of anyon `a`. -/
  chi : A → AddChar A ℂ
  /-- The braiding is bilinear: `χ_{a+a'} = χ_a · χ_{a'}`. -/
  map_add' : ∀ a a', chi (a + a') = chi a * chi a'
  /-- Nondegeneracy: only the vacuum braids trivially with everything. -/
  nondeg : ∀ a, chi a = 0 → a = 0

namespace ModularBraiding

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A] [Fintype A] (M : ModularBraiding A)

-- !-- `χ_0 = χ_0 · χ_0` forces `χ_0 = 1`, the trivial character. -- !--
/-- The vacuum braids trivially: `χ_0` is the trivial character. -/
lemma map_zero : M.chi 0 = 0 := by
  have h := M.map_add' 0 0
  rw [add_zero] at h
  have h2 : M.chi 0 * M.chi 0 = 1 * M.chi 0 := by rw [one_mul]; exact h.symm
  rw [mul_right_cancel h2, AddChar.one_eq_zero]

-- !-- From `χ_a · χ_{-a} = χ_0 = 1` we read off `χ_{-a} = χ_a⁻¹`. -- !--
/-- Antipode: `χ_{-a} = χ_a⁻¹`. -/
lemma map_neg (a : A) : M.chi (-a) = (M.chi a)⁻¹ := by
  have h := M.map_add' a (-a)
  rw [add_neg_cancel, M.map_zero, ← AddChar.one_eq_zero] at h
  exact eq_inv_of_mul_eq_one_left (by rw [mul_comm]; exact h.symm)

-- !-- If `χ_a = χ_b` then `χ_{a-b} = 1`, so nondegeneracy gives `a = b`. -- !--
/-- Nondegeneracy makes the assignment `a ↦ χ_a` injective. -/
lemma chi_injective : Function.Injective M.chi := by
  intro a b hab
  have hz : M.chi (a - b) = 0 := by
    rw [sub_eq_add_neg, M.map_add', M.map_neg, hab, mul_inv_cancel, AddChar.one_eq_zero]
  exact sub_eq_zero.mp (M.nondeg _ hz)

/-- `χ_a · χ_b⁻¹` is the trivial character iff `a = b`. -/
lemma chi_diff_eq_zero_iff (a b : A) : M.chi a * (M.chi b)⁻¹ = 0 ↔ a = b := by
  rw [← AddChar.one_eq_zero, mul_inv_eq_one]
  exact ⟨fun h => M.chi_injective h, fun h => by rw [h]⟩

-- !-- `χ_a(c) · conj χ_b(c) = (χ_a · χ_b⁻¹)(c)`; summing and using `AddChar.sum_eq_ite`
--     (character orthogonality) gives `|A|` if `a = b` and `0` otherwise. -- !--
/-- **Character orthogonality.** The rows of the braiding character table are
    orthogonal: `∑_c χ_a(c) · conj χ_b(c) = |A| · δ_{a,b}`. -/
theorem chi_orthogonality [DecidableEq A] (a b : A) :
    ∑ c, M.chi a c * conj (M.chi b c) = if a = b then (Fintype.card A : ℂ) else 0 := by
  classical
  have key : ∀ c, M.chi a c * conj (M.chi b c) = (M.chi a * (M.chi b)⁻¹) c := by
    intro c
    rw [AddChar.coe_mul]
    simp only [Pi.mul_apply]
    rw [AddChar.inv_apply', ← AddChar.inv_apply_eq_conj]
  simp_rw [key]
  rw [AddChar.sum_eq_ite]
  exact if_congr (M.chi_diff_eq_zero_iff a b) rfl rfl

/-- The modular **S-matrix** entry `S_{a,b} = (1/√d) · χ_a(b)` with `d = |A|`. -/
noncomputable def Smatrix (a b : A) : ℂ := (1 / Real.sqrt (Fintype.card A)) * M.chi a b

-- !-- Pull out the constant `(1/√d)·conj(1/√d) = 1/d` from each summand and apply
--     `chi_orthogonality`; the `1/d · |A|` collapses to `1` on the diagonal. -- !--
/-- **Unitarity of the modular S-matrix.** `∑_c S_{a,c} · conj S_{b,c} = δ_{a,b}`,
    i.e. `S S† = 1`.  This is the central structural property of modular data. -/
theorem smatrix_unitary [DecidableEq A] (a b : A) :
    ∑ c, M.Smatrix a c * conj (M.Smatrix b c) = if a = b then (1 : ℂ) else 0 := by
  have hd : (0 : ℝ) < Fintype.card A := by exact_mod_cast Fintype.card_pos
  have hsq : (1 / (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card A) : ℂ)) * (1 / (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card A) : ℂ))
      = 1 / (Fintype.card A : ℂ) := by
    rw [div_mul_div_comm, one_mul, ← Complex.ofReal_mul, Real.mul_self_sqrt hd.le,
      Complex.ofReal_natCast]
  have hcr : conj (1 / (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card A) : ℂ)) = 1 / (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card A) : ℂ) := by
    rw [map_div₀, map_one, Complex.conj_ofReal]
  have step : ∀ c, M.Smatrix a c * conj (M.Smatrix b c)
      = (1 / (Fintype.card A : ℂ)) * (M.chi a c * conj (M.chi b c)) := by
    intro c
    rw [Smatrix, Smatrix, map_mul, hcr, mul_mul_mul_comm, hsq]
  simp_rw [step]
  rw [← Finset.mul_sum, M.chi_orthogonality a b]
  by_cases h : a = b
  · simp only [h, if_true]
    rw [div_mul_cancel₀]
    exact_mod_cast Fintype.card_ne_zero
  · simp only [h, if_false, mul_zero]

end ModularBraiding

/-! ## Section 3: The Cyclic Anyon Model `ZMod n` — a Fully Worked Example

We now *construct* a modular braiding on `A = ZMod n` from the standard additive
character `j ↦ exp(2πi j / n)`, realizing the discrete Fourier matrix and upgrading
the abstract unitarity theorem to an unconditional statement. -/

-- !-- Take `χ_a = mulShift stdAddChar a` (so `χ_a(b) = exp(2πi a b / n)`); bilinearity is
--     `AddChar.mulShift_mul` and nondegeneracy is primitivity of `stdAddChar`. -- !--
/-- The **cyclic anyon braiding** on `ZMod n`: `χ_a(b) = exp(2πi a b / n)`, built from
    `ZMod.stdAddChar`.  Bilinearity is `mulShift_mul`; nondegeneracy is primitivity. -/
noncomputable def cyclicBraiding (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] : ModularBraiding (ZMod n) where
  chi a := (ZMod.stdAddChar (N := n)).mulShift a
  map_add' a a' := (AddChar.mulShift_mul _ a a').symm
  nondeg a h := by
    by_contra ha
    rw [← AddChar.one_eq_zero] at h
    exact ZMod.isPrimitive_stdAddChar n ha h

-- !-- Unfold `Smatrix` and `mulShift_apply`: the braiding entry is `exp(2πi a b / n)`. -- !--
/-- The cyclic S-matrix is the **discrete Fourier matrix**
    `S_{a,b} = (1/√n) · exp(2πi a b / n)`. -/
theorem cyclicBraiding_Smatrix (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (a b : ZMod n) :
    (cyclicBraiding n).Smatrix a b
      = (1 / Real.sqrt (Fintype.card (ZMod n))) * ZMod.stdAddChar (a * b) := by
  rw [ModularBraiding.Smatrix]
  rfl

-- !-- Direct corollary of `smatrix_unitary` applied to the constructed `cyclicBraiding`. -- !--
/-- **Unconditional unitarity** of the cyclic (discrete-Fourier) S-matrix. -/
theorem cyclic_smatrix_unitary (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (a b : ZMod n) :
    ∑ c, (cyclicBraiding n).Smatrix a c * conj ((cyclicBraiding n).Smatrix b c)
      = if a = b then (1 : ℂ) else 0 :=
  (cyclicBraiding n).smatrix_unitary a b

-- !-- Toric-code matching: with `A = ZMod 2 × ZMod 2` we recover `GSD = 4^g`, and `4`
--     on the torus, matching `ToricCode.ground_space_dim`. -- !--
/-- **Bridge to the toric code.** The four-anyon theory `(ZMod 2)²` has genus-`g`
    degeneracy `4^g`; on the torus this is `4`, matching `ToricCode.ground_space_dim`. -/
theorem toricCode_GSD (g : ℕ) : GSD (ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) g = 4 ^ g := by
  rw [GSD]
  norm_num

/-- On the torus the `(ZMod 2)²` toric code has the expected `4`-fold degeneracy. -/
theorem toricCode_torus_GSD : GSD (ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) 1 = 4 := by
  rw [toricCode_GSD]; norm_num

/-! ## Section 4: Examples and a Boundary Case -/

example (g : ℕ) : GSD (ZMod 5) g = 5 ^ g := by rw [GSD]; norm_num

example : GSD (ZMod 3) 2 = 9 := by rw [GSD]; norm_num

-- !-- Boundary: on the sphere (`g = 0`) every abelian theory has a unique ground state. -- !--
/-- **Boundary case.** On the sphere (`g = 0`) the ground state is *unique*
    (`GSD = 1`) for every abelian theory — there is no topological degeneracy. -/
example [Fintype A] : GSD A 0 = 1 := by rw [GSD, pow_zero]

end TopologicalOrderGenus

`Bridges/EmergentRicciFlow.lean`.

Computed directly (`critic M c := least D with M ≤ D^c`):

These match `D_c = ⌈M^{1/c}⌉`, i.e. the bond dimension needed so that the cut
Hilbert space `D^c` first reaches the bulk dimension `M`. More cut bonds (larger
`c`, a "thicker" minimal surface) sharply lowers the required bond dimension —
the discrete analogue of the Ryu–Takayanagi area law.

## 2. Sharpness of the transition (width exactly one in `D`)

For `D = D_c` the bulk is resolved; for `D = D_c − 1` it is not:

| `M` | `c` | `D_c` | resolves at `D_c−1`? | resolves at `D_c`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100  | 3 | 5 | false | true |
| 256  | 4 | 4 | false | true |
| 1000 | 5 | 4 | false | true |

This is the computational witness of `critical_is_sharp`: the resolution predicate
flips exactly once, with no intermediate regime — a first-order ("sharp") transition.

## 3. Ricci-flow dichotomy across `D_c`

With contraction factor `q = flowFactor D_c D = D_c / D` and flow
`g_{n+1} = q · g_n` (closed form `g_n = q^n g_0`):

| regime | `D` vs `D_c` | `q = D_c/D` | flow `q^n g_0` | geometry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| super-critical | `D > D_c` | `< 1` | `→ 0` | converges → smooth |
| critical       | `D = D_c` | `= 1` | constant | marginal (transition) |
| sub-critical   | `D < D_c` | `> 1` | `→ +∞` | diverges → fractal |

E.g. `D_c = 5, D = 10`: `q = 0.5`, `g_n = 0.5^n g_0 → 0` (smooth).
`D_c = 5, D = 2`: `q = 2.5`, `g_n = 2.5^n g_0 → ∞` (fractal).

# Future Directions

These directions build on the negative/control theorem in
`Catalog/Bridges/UniformBondScaling.lean`, which shows that uniform
bond-dimension scaling preserves the set of minimum cuts on a fixed graph.

## 1. Nonuniform scaling profiles and the first argmin flip

Replace the single global factor `D` by a per-edge profile `D_e = g_e(t)` driven
by one shared parameter `t`, and study the smallest `t` at which the minimizing
cut changes. The key insight is that homogeneity — the property that made the
argmin invariant — is destroyed precisely when two edges scale at different
rates, so the transition threshold becomes the first `t` where two distinct cuts
tie in capacity, an event governed by the difference of two affine (or monotone)
functions of `t`. This reframes "phase transition" as a piecewise structure on
the parameter line with finitely many breakpoints, each computable from cut
capacity differences. Why now? The uniform case is fully formalized, so the
nonuniform extension is a clean, well-scoped next theorem rather than an
open-ended modeling exercise, and the breakpoint count is a finite, decidable
quantity ready for a Lean development.

## 2. Topology change through capacity-floor rank defects

Model rank defects by deleting an edge whenever its scaled capacity would fall
below an integer floor, so that the graph's edge set itself depends on `D`.
The key insight is that this couples the combinatorial object (which edges exist) to the numerical knob (the bond dimension), which is exactly the ingredient our control theorem proves is missing in the uniform model — and once edges can vanish, min-cut surfaces really can jump homotopy class.
A minimal worked example
(say two parallel paths of different lengths, one of which loses an edge first)
would exhibit a genuine, provable min-cut transition. Why now? Our formalization
already provides `cutCap`, `IsMinCut`, and the complete-graph closed form, so a
defect model can be layered on top with the invariance theorem as the explicit
baseline it must violate.

## 3. Concave capacity laws and additive per-bond offsets

Study capacities of the form `c_e(D) = f(D) + b_e` for a strictly concave
monotone `f` (e.g. `log`) and fixed per-bond offsets `b_e`. The key insight is
that pure `f(D)` scaling remains monotone and therefore argmin-invariant by the
same reasoning as our theorem, so any transition must be carried entirely by the
*offsets*, which decouple from `D` and create a tie-crossing as `f(D)` grows. This
pinpoints offsets — not the concave law itself — as the operative degree of
freedom, sharpening folklore about `log D` entropy heuristics. Why now? The
real-valued generalization of `cutCap` is a direct port of the natural-number
version we proved, and Mathlib's order and monotonicity lemmas make the concave
monotone step routine to formalize.

## 4. Max-flow value and weighted vertex cuts

Extend the invariance question from edge min-cuts to the max-flow value and to
weighted vertex cuts, asking whether positive homogeneity still forces the
optimizer set to be scaling-invariant. The key insight is that max-flow/min-cut
duality means the flow value inherits the degree-one homogeneity of capacities,
so the same order-isomorphism argument should transport verbatim, giving a second
control theorem for the dual object. Establishing this rules out an even broader
family of "bond-dimension drives the transition" claims in one stroke. Why now?
Mathlib has growing flow-network infrastructure, and our cut-capacity definitions
are deliberately elementary, so aligning them with a max-flow formulation is a
natural and timely consolidation.

## 5. Random ensembles and the disappearance of transitions on average

Place a distribution on base weights `w` and ask how the (now random) min-cut
identity behaves under uniform scaling. The key insight is that since scaling
preserves the argmin *pointwise* for every realization, it must also preserve it
*almost surely*, so any apparent transition seen in random-tensor-network
simulations cannot be an artifact of the bond-dimension sweep and must instead
track a changing base distribution or topology. Formalizing this turns a
qualitative cautionary statement about numerics into a provable measure-theoretic
invariance. Why now? With the deterministic invariance proved, the probabilistic
lift is a thin wrapper, and it directly addresses how practitioners interpret
bond-dimension scans in random-tensor toy models of holography.

# Uniform Bond-Dimension Scaling Cannot Create a Min-Cut Phase Transition

## Problem statement

In holographic and tensor-network approaches to emergent geometry, the
entanglement entropy of a boundary region is frequently estimated by a *min-cut*
through the network: the minimum total bond weight that must be severed to
separate the region from its complement (a Ryu–Takayanagi–style discrete
surface). A common heuristic assigns each bond a capacity that is a monotone
function of its bond dimension `D` — often proportional to `log D`, or simply to
`D` itself in a coarse counting model.

This invites a tempting narrative: by *increasing the bond dimension uniformly*
one might drive the network through a sharp transition in which the dominant
min-cut surface jumps from one homotopy class to another, producing a phase
transition in the reconstructed geometry.

We show, rigorously and in full formal detail, that this cannot happen in the
fixed-topology, uniform-`D` model. Uniform bond-dimension scaling multiplies the
capacity of **every** cut by the same positive scalar, so the *set of minimizing
cuts is exactly preserved*. No threshold value of `D` can change which cut is
minimal. Any genuine min-cut phase transition must come from some *other*
changing ingredient — graph topology, nonuniform capacities, random rank
defects, or a different geometric reconstruction map — not from the bond
dimension alone.

The result is a negative/control theorem. It does not assert that tensor networks
fail to produce emergent geometry; it isolates and excludes one specific,
frequently-invoked mechanism.

## Definitions

Throughout, `V` is a finite vertex type with decidable equality, and a weighted
directed graph is a function `w : V → V → ℕ`.

* **Cut capacity.** For a subset `S : Finset V`,
  `cutCap w S = ∑ x ∈ S, ∑ y ∉ S, w x y`,
  the total weight of edges directed from `S` to its complement.

* **Uniform scaling.** For `D : ℕ`,
  `scaleWeight D w = fun x y => D * w x y`.

* **Minimum cut.** `IsMinCut w S` holds iff `∀ T, cutCap w S ≤ cutCap w T`.

* **Complete unit-weight graph.** `completeUnitWeight x y = if x = y then 0 else 1`.

## Main theorems

All statements are formalized and proved without `sorry`, `admit`, or new axioms
in `Catalog/Bridges/UniformBondScaling.lean`.

1. **`cutCap_scale`.** `cutCap (scaleWeight D w) S = D * cutCap w S`.

2. **`cutCap_scale_le_iff`.** If `0 < D` then
   `cutCap (scaleWeight D w) S ≤ cutCap (scaleWeight D w) T ↔ cutCap w S ≤ cutCap w T`.

3. **`isMinCut_scale_iff`.** If `0 < D` then
   `IsMinCut (scaleWeight D w) S ↔ IsMinCut w S`.

4. **`no_uniform_bond_dimension_threshold`** (main result). For any positive
   `D1, D2`,
   `IsMinCut (scaleWeight D1 w) S ↔ IsMinCut (scaleWeight D2 w) S`.

5. **`cutCap_completeUnitWeight`** (closed form).
   `cutCap completeUnitWeight S = S.card * (Fintype.card V − S.card)`.

## Proof sketches

* **`cutCap_scale`.** The factor `D` is constant in both summation indices, so it
  pulls out of the inner and outer sums by `Finset.mul_sum` applied twice.

* **`cutCap_scale_le_iff`.** Rewrite both sides with `cutCap_scale`, reducing the
  claim to `D * a ≤ D * b ↔ a ≤ b`, which holds for positive `D`
  (`Nat.mul_le_mul_left_iff`).

* **`isMinCut_scale_iff`.** `IsMinCut` is a universally quantified inequality over
  all cuts `T`; apply `cutCap_scale_le_iff` pointwise inside `forall_congr'`.

* **`no_uniform_bond_dimension_threshold`.** Rewrite both sides via
  `isMinCut_scale_iff`; each reduces to the *same* unscaled statement
  `IsMinCut w S`, so the two are equivalent. In particular the set of minimizers
  is independent of the positive scaling factor.

* **`cutCap_completeUnitWeight`.** The inner filter `{y | y ∉ S}` is the
  complement `Sᶜ`, of cardinality `Fintype.card V − S.card`. For `x ∈ S` and
  `y ∉ S` we always have `x ≠ y`, so every summand equals `1`; the inner sum is
  the size of the complement, and summing the constant over `S` gives
  `S.card * (Fintype.card V − S.card)`.

## Significance

The min-cut/max-flow picture is central to discrete holography: it underlies
Ryu–Takayanagi entropy estimates, holographic codes, and random-tensor-network
toy models of AdS/CFT. Because cut capacity is *positively homogeneous of degree
one* in the edge weights, scaling all bond dimensions by a common factor is an
order-isomorphism on the lattice of cut capacities. The argmin is therefore a
scaling invariant. This makes precise the intuition that "turning a global knob"
cannot, by itself, reorganize which surface is minimal — a useful sanity check
and a guardrail against over-interpreting numerical bond-dimension sweeps.

## Open questions

* **Nonuniform scaling.** If different bonds scale with different exponents of a
  shared parameter, when does the argmin first change, and can the threshold be
  characterized combinatorially?
* **Topology change.** Adding or deleting edges as `D` grows (e.g. rank defects
  appearing below a capacity floor) breaks homogeneity; what is the minimal model
  exhibiting a genuine min-cut transition?
* **Concave capacities.** With capacity `f(D)` for a strictly concave monotone
  `f` (such as `log`), uniform scaling is still monotone, so the argmin is again
  invariant; what additional structure (e.g. additive offsets per bond) is needed
  to create a transition?
* **Real-weighted and max-flow formulations.** Does the same invariance persist
  for real capacities and the max-flow value, and for weighted vertex cuts?

import Algebra.LibraryOfBabel

/-!
# The Library of Babel: proof sets and the universal catalog

This file extends `Algebra/LibraryOfBabel.lean` to the setting of the problem
statement, where a theorem `T` is associated to a *set* `ℙ_T` of valid proof
strings (all of the same length `k = ℓ(T)`), rather than a single pattern.

Main results:

* `prob_containsAny_bound` : **Theorem 2 (general union bound).** The probability
  that a uniformly random volume contains *some* proof from a finite set
  `P ⊆ Σ^k` is at most `|P| · (L - k + 1) · b^{-k}`.
* `prob_containsAny_sparse_bound` : **Theorem 2 (sparse corollary).** If
  `|P| ≤ c`, then this probability is at most `c · (L - k + 1) · b^{-k}`, matching
  the bound `P_T ≤ c·(N-ℓ+1)·25^{-ℓ}` from the problem statement.
* `catalog_mono`, `catalog_union` : **Theorem 4 (catalog structure).** The catalog
  map `C(T) = { v : v contains a proof of T }` is monotone in the proof set and
  sends unions of proof sets to unions of catalogs, i.e. its image is closed under
  finite unions (a sub-`∪`-semilattice of `𝒫(L)`).
* `card_contains_inter_le` : **Theorem 4 (overlap bound).** For two single proof
  strings `p₁ ∈ Σ^{k₁}`, `p₂ ∈ Σ^{k₂}`, the number of volumes containing *both* is
  at most `(L - k₁ + 1) · (L - k₂ + 1) · b^{L - max k₁ k₂}`.

  *Remark.* The bound `|C(T₁) ∩ C(T₂)| ≤ 25^{N - max(ℓ₁,ℓ₂) + 1}` stated in the
  problem is **false** as written: it omits the number of admissible window
  positions, which contributes the factor `(L - k₁ + 1)(L - k₂ + 1)`. The
  statement here is the corrected, true overlap bound, obtained by a union bound
  over all pairs of window positions, each pair contributing at most
  `b^{L - max k₁ k₂}` volumes (the joint event is contained in the single-window
  event for the *longer* of the two proofs).

* `babel_prob_bound` : the concrete instantiation with the alphabet size `b = 25`
  and library length `N = 1312000` from the problem statement.
-/

open Finset

open scoped Classical

namespace LibraryOfBabel

/-! ### Proof sets and the "contains some proof" event -/

/-- A volume `v` contains *some* proof from the finite proof set `P` (of length-`k`
strings): there is a `p ∈ P` occurring as a contiguous substring of `v`. -/
def ContainsAny {b L k : ℕ} (P : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)) (v : Volume b L) : Prop :=
  ∃ p ∈ P, Contains p v

/-! ### Theorem 2: union bound over a proof set -/

/-
**Theorem 2 (general union bound).** The probability that a uniformly random
volume of length `L` contains some proof from a finite set `P ⊆ Σ^k` (with
`k ≤ L`) is at most `|P| · (L - k + 1) · b^{-k}`.
-/
theorem prob_containsAny_bound {b k : ℕ} (L : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ L)
    (P : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)) :
    ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v : Volume b L | ContainsAny P v}
      ≤ (P.card : ℝ) * (((L - k + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) * (b : ℝ) ^ (-(k : ℤ))) := by
  by_contra! h_contra;
  -- Apply the union bound to the probability.
  have h_union_bound : ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v | ContainsAny P v} ≤ ∑ p ∈ P, ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v | Contains p v} := by
    -- By definition of `ProbabilityTheory.prob`, we can rewrite the left-hand side as the sum of the probabilities of the individual events.
    have h_lhs : ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v | ContainsAny P v} = (Finset.univ.filter (fun v : Volume b L => ∃ p ∈ P, Contains p v)).card / (Library b L).card := by
      convert rfl;
      congr;
    -- By definition of `ProbabilityTheory.prob`, we can rewrite the right-hand side as the sum of the probabilities of the individual events.
    have h_rhs : ∑ p ∈ P, ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v | Contains p v} = (∑ p ∈ P, (Finset.univ.filter (fun v : Volume b L => Contains p v)).card) / (Library b L).card := by
      simp +decide [ ProbabilityTheory.prob, Finset.sum_div _ _ _ ];
      rfl;
    rw [ h_lhs, h_rhs ];
    gcongr;
    exact Finset.card_le_card ( show Finset.filter ( fun v => ∃ p ∈ P, Contains p v ) Finset.univ ⊆ Finset.biUnion P ( fun p => Finset.filter ( fun v => Contains p v ) Finset.univ ) from fun x hx => by aesop ) |> le_trans <| Finset.card_biUnion_le;
  refine h_contra.not_ge <| h_union_bound.trans <| ?_;
  refine' le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun p hp => prob_contains_substring_bound L hk p ) _ ; norm_num

/-
**Theorem 2 (sparse corollary).** If the proof set is sparse, `|P| ≤ c`, then
the probability that a random volume contains a proof is at most
`c · (L - k + 1) · b^{-k}`. This is the bound `P_T ≤ c·(N-ℓ+1)·25^{-ℓ}` from the
problem statement (with the sparsity constant interpreted as a bound on `|ℙ_T|`).
-/
theorem prob_containsAny_sparse_bound {b k : ℕ} (L : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ L) (c : ℝ)
    (P : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)) (hP : (P.card : ℝ) ≤ c) :
    ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library b L) {v : Volume b L | ContainsAny P v}
      ≤ c * (((L - k + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) * (b : ℝ) ^ (-(k : ℤ))) := by
  exact le_trans ( @LibraryOfBabel.prob_containsAny_bound b k L hk P ) ( by gcongr )

/-! ### Theorem 4: the universal catalog -/

/-- The catalog map `C(T)`: the set of volumes containing some proof from `P`. -/
def Catalog {b k : ℕ} (L : ℕ) (P : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)) : Set (Volume b L) :=
  {v | ContainsAny P v}

/-
**Theorem 4 (monotonicity).** A larger proof set yields a larger catalog.
-/
theorem catalog_mono {b k L : ℕ} {P Q : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)} (h : P ⊆ Q) :
    Catalog L P ⊆ Catalog L Q := by
  exact fun v hv => by obtain ⟨ p, hp, hp' ⟩ := hv; exact ⟨ p, h hp, hp' ⟩ ;

/-
**Theorem 4 (sub-union-semilattice).** The catalog of a union of proof sets is
the union of the catalogs; hence the image of `C` is closed under finite unions.
-/
theorem catalog_union {b k L : ℕ} (P Q : Finset (Fin k → Fin b)) :
    Catalog L (P ∪ Q) = Catalog L P ∪ Catalog L Q := by
  ext v
  simp [Catalog, ContainsAny];
  grind

/-
The number of volumes in which `p₁` occurs at position `i` *and* `p₂` occurs at
position `j` is at most `b^{L - max k₁ k₂}`: the joint event is contained in the
single-window event for the longer of the two proofs.
-/
theorem card_occursAt_pair_le {b L k₁ k₂ : ℕ} (p₁ : Fin k₁ → Fin b) (p₂ : Fin k₂ → Fin b)
    (i j : ℕ) (hi : i + k₁ ≤ L) (hj : j + k₂ ≤ L) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun v : Volume b L => OccursAt p₁ v i ∧ OccursAt p₂ v j)).card
      ≤ b ^ (L - max k₁ k₂) := by
  by_cases hk₁ : k₁ ≥ k₂ <;> simp_all +decide [ OccursAt ];
  · refine' le_trans ( Finset.card_le_card _ ) _;
    exact Finset.univ.filter fun v => ∀ j : Fin k₁, readAt v ( i + j ) = some ( p₁ j );
    · grind;
    · convert card_occursAt p₁ i hi |> le_of_eq using 1;
  · refine' le_trans ( Finset.card_le_card _ ) _;
    exact Finset.univ.filter fun v => ∀ j_1 : Fin k₂, readAt v ( j + j_1 ) = some ( p₂ j_1 );
    · grind;
    · rw [ max_eq_right hk₁.le ];
      convert card_occursAt p₂ j hj |> le_of_eq using 1

/-
**Theorem 4 (overlap bound, corrected).** The number of volumes containing both
a proof string `p₁ ∈ Σ^{k₁}` and a proof string `p₂ ∈ Σ^{k₂}` is at most
`(L - k₁ + 1) · (L - k₂ + 1) · b^{L - max k₁ k₂}`.
-/
theorem card_contains_inter_le {b L k₁ k₂ : ℕ} (hk₁ : k₁ ≤ L) (hk₂ : k₂ ≤ L)
    (p₁ : Fin k₁ → Fin b) (p₂ : Fin k₂ → Fin b) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun v : Volume b L => Contains p₁ v ∧ Contains p₂ v)).card
      ≤ (L - k₁ + 1) * (L - k₂ + 1) * b ^ (L - max k₁ k₂) := by
  -- The set `{v | Contains p₁ v ∧ Contains p₂ v}` is contained in the double union over valid window positions `i ∈ range (L - k₁ + 1)`, `j ∈ range (L - k₂ + 1)` of `{v | OccursAt p₁ v i ∧ OccursAt p₂ v j}`.
  have h_subset : (Finset.univ.filter (fun v : (Volume b L) => Contains p₁ v ∧ Contains p₂ v)) ⊆ (Finset.biUnion (Finset.range (L - k₁ + 1)) fun i => Finset.biUnion (Finset.range (L - k₂ + 1)) fun j => Finset.univ.filter (fun v : (Volume b L) => OccursAt p₁ v i ∧ OccursAt p₂ v j)) := by
    intro v hv;
    obtain ⟨i₁, hi₁⟩ : ∃ i₁, OccursAt p₁ v i₁ ∧ i₁ + k₁ ≤ L := by
      obtain ⟨ i₁, hi₁ ⟩ := Finset.mem_filter.mp hv |>.2.1;
      by_cases h : k₁ = 0;
      · unfold OccursAt; aesop;
      · exact ⟨ i₁, hi₁, by have := hi₁ ⟨ k₁ - 1, Nat.sub_lt ( Nat.pos_of_ne_zero h ) zero_lt_one ⟩ ; rw [ readAt ] at this; split_ifs at this ; norm_num at * ; linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr h ) ] ⟩
    obtain ⟨i₂, hi₂⟩ : ∃ i₂, OccursAt p₂ v i₂ ∧ i₂ + k₂ ≤ L := by
      rcases Finset.mem_filter.mp hv |>.2 |>.2 with ⟨ i₂, hi₂ ⟩;
      by_cases hi₂' : i₂ + k₂ ≤ L;
      · use i₂;
      · rcases k₂ with ( _ | k₂ ) <;> simp_all +decide [ OccursAt ];
        · exact ⟨ L, le_rfl ⟩;
        · specialize hi₂ ⟨ k₂, by linarith ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ readAt ];
          linarith [ hi₂.choose ];
    exact Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨ i₁, Finset.mem_range.mpr ( by omega ), Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨ i₂, Finset.mem_range.mpr ( by omega ), by aesop ⟩ ⟩;
  refine le_trans ( Finset.card_le_card h_subset ) ?_;
  refine' le_trans ( Finset.card_biUnion_le ) _;
  refine' le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => Finset.card_biUnion_le ) _;
  refine' le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => Finset.sum_le_sum fun j hj => card_occursAt_pair_le p₁ p₂ i j ( by linarith [ Finset.mem_range.mp hi, Nat.sub_add_cancel hk₁ ] ) ( by linarith [ Finset.mem_range.mp hj, Nat.sub_add_cancel hk₂ ] ) ) _ ; norm_num [ mul_assoc ]

/-! ### Concrete instantiation: 25 symbols, 1312000 pages -/

/-- The Library of Babel of the problem statement: `b = 25` symbols, `N = 1312000`
positions, containing exactly `25 ^ 1312000` volumes. -/
theorem babel_card_library : (Library 25 1312000).card = 25 ^ 1312000 :=
  card_library 25 1312000

/-- **Concrete Theorem 2.** In the `25`-symbol, `1312000`-page Library of Babel, the
probability that a random volume contains a fixed proof string of length `k` is at
most `(1312000 - k + 1) · 25^{-k}`. -/
theorem babel_prob_bound (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ 1312000) (pattern : Fin k → Fin 25) :
    ProbabilityTheory.prob (Library 25 1312000) {v : Volume 25 1312000 | Contains pattern v}
      ≤ ((1312000 - k + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) * (25 : ℝ) ^ (-(k : ℤ)) :=
  prob_contains_substring_bound 1312000 hk pattern

end LibraryOfBabel

/-
  Chaos and the Three-Body Problem: Lyapunov Exponent Bounds
  ==========================================================

  The gravitational three-body problem is the canonical example of deterministic
  chaos: its flow has a strictly positive maximal Lyapunov exponent, so nearby
  trajectories separate exponentially fast. Formalizing the full Hamiltonian flow
  is out of reach of current Mathlib, so we formalize the *rigorous analytic core*
  of the phenomenon for smooth iterated maps — the setting in which positivity of
  Lyapunov exponents is actually provable and which captures every essential
  feature of chaos in the three-body problem:

  * the multiplicative (cocycle) structure of the derivative of an iterate,
  * exponential divergence of nearby orbits for uniformly expanding maps,
  * strict positivity of the (finite-time) maximal Lyapunov exponent, and
  * the Pesin / variational bridge between the Lyapunov exponent and entropy.

  The Birkhoff-sum identity `log_abs_deriv_iterate_eq_sum` is the discrete-time
  shadow of the variational equation governing the separation of three-body
  trajectories; positivity (`ftle_ge_log`) is the statement that the system is
  chaotic.

  Main results:
  1. `deriv_iterate_eq_prod`      — derivative of the n-th iterate is the orbit product (chain rule).
  2. `log_abs_deriv_iterate_eq_sum` — log of the stretching factor is a Birkhoff sum of `log|f'|`.
  3. `abs_deriv_iterate_ge`       — uniform expansion forces exponential growth `cⁿ`.
  4. `ftle_ge_log`                — the finite-time Lyapunov exponent is ≥ log c > 0 (CHAOS).
  5. `ftle_eq_log_of_uniform`     — exact Lyapunov exponent log c for constant-stretch maps.
  6. `entropy_periodic_growth`    — periodic-orbit growth rate (entropy) of the degree-d map is log d.
  7. `pesin_identity_uniform_model` — Pesin's formula: entropy = Lyapunov exponent = log d.

  Catalog synthesis: this complements `Catalog/Shared/HorseshoeComputation.lean`
  and `Catalog/Shared/SymbolicDynamics` (symbolic/topological chaos) and the
  tropical Lyapunov material in `Catalog/Tropical/TropicalDeepResearch.lean` by
  supplying the *smooth/analytic* Lyapunov-exponent theory and its entropy bridge.
-/
import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open Filter Topology Finset

namespace LyapunovChaos

/-- Finite-time Lyapunov exponent of `f` at `x` over `n` steps: the average
exponential stretching rate of the derivative of the `n`-th iterate. The maximal
Lyapunov exponent of a chaotic system (such as the three-body problem) is the
`limsup` of this quantity; strict positivity is the hallmark of chaos. -/
def ftle (f : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  Real.log |deriv (f^[n]) x| / n

/-- Number of period-`n` points of the degree-`d` uniformly expanding circle map
`x ↦ d·x mod 1`. There are `dⁿ - 1` of them; their exponential growth rate is the
topological entropy of the map. -/
def periodicPointCount (d n : ℕ) : ℕ := d ^ n - 1

/-
!-- The derivative of the n-th iterate factors as a product along the orbit
by the chain rule (induction via `iterate_succ'` and `deriv_comp`). -- !--

**Chain rule for iterates.** The derivative of the `n`-th iterate of `f` at `x`
is the product of the derivatives of `f` taken along the forward orbit of `x`. This
is the multiplicative cocycle underlying every Lyapunov-exponent computation.
-/
theorem deriv_iterate_eq_prod (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    deriv (f^[n]) x = ∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, deriv f (f^[i] x) := by
  induction' n with n ih generalizing x;
  · norm_num;
  · convert deriv_comp _ ( hf _ ) ( show DifferentiableAt ℝ ( f^[n] ) x from ?_ ) using 1;
    · rw [ Function.iterate_succ' ];
    · rw [ Finset.prod_range_succ, ih, mul_comm ];
    · exact hf.iterate n x

/-
!-- Take logs of absolute values in `deriv_iterate_eq_prod`; `Real.log_prod`
applies since each factor is nonzero. -- !--

**Birkhoff-sum form of the stretching factor.** The logarithm of the absolute
stretching factor `|(fⁿ)'(x)|` equals the Birkhoff sum of `log|f'|` along the orbit.
This is the discrete-time variational equation for orbit separation.
-/
theorem log_abs_deriv_iterate_eq_sum (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f)
    (hne : ∀ y, deriv f y ≠ 0) (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    Real.log |deriv (f^[n]) x| = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, Real.log |deriv f (f^[i] x)| := by
  rw [ ← Real.log_prod, deriv_iterate_eq_prod f hf ];
  · rw [ Finset.abs_prod ];
  · aesop

/-
!-- The product form plus `Finset.prod_le_prod` with the uniform lower bound c
gives the geometric lower bound cⁿ. -- !--

**Exponential divergence.** If `f` stretches lengths by at least a factor
`c ≥ 0` everywhere, then the `n`-th iterate stretches by at least `cⁿ`. For `c > 1`
this is exponential sensitivity to initial conditions.
-/
theorem abs_deriv_iterate_ge (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) {c : ℝ}
    (hc0 : 0 ≤ c) (hc : ∀ y, c ≤ |deriv f y|) (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    c ^ n ≤ |deriv (f^[n]) x| := by
  rw [ deriv_iterate_eq_prod ];
  · rw [ Finset.abs_prod ] ; exact le_trans ( by norm_num ) ( Finset.prod_le_prod ( fun _ _ => by positivity ) fun _ _ => hc _ ) ;
  · assumption

/-
!-- From abs_deriv_iterate_ge, log|(fⁿ)'(x)| ≥ n·log c; dividing by n≥1 gives
ftle ≥ log c, and log c > 0 since c > 1. -- !--

**Positivity of the maximal Lyapunov exponent ⇒ deterministic chaos.** For a
uniformly expanding map (`|f'| ≥ c > 1`), every finite-time Lyapunov exponent is at
least `log c > 0`. This is the rigorous statement that such a system is chaotic.
-/
theorem ftle_ge_log (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) {c : ℝ} (hc : 1 < c)
    (hbound : ∀ y, c ≤ |deriv f y|) {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) (x : ℝ) :
    Real.log c ≤ ftle f x n := by
  convert div_le_div_of_nonneg_right ( Real.log_le_log ( by positivity ) ( abs_deriv_iterate_ge f hf ( by positivity ) hbound n x ) ) ( Nat.cast_nonneg n ) using 1;
  rw [ Real.log_pow, mul_div_cancel_left₀ _ ( by positivity ) ]

/-
**Strict positivity.** Under uniform expansion the finite-time Lyapunov
exponent is strictly positive.
-/
theorem ftle_pos (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Differentiable ℝ f) {c : ℝ} (hc : 1 < c)

This module develops the algebraic framework connecting finite group character

* `CharacterTable.sum_dim_sq_eq_order`: The sum of squared irreducible
  representation dimensions equals the group order (Burnside's theorem).
* `MoonshineDatum.multiplicity_recovery`: Character orthogonality allows
  recovery of graded multiplicities from McKay-Thompson coefficients.
* `MoonshineDatum.mckay_trace_bound`: McKay-Thompson coefficients are bounded

* `MoonshineDatum.moonshine_inner_product_identity`: The inner product of
  McKay-Thompson coefficients at different grades computes a representation-

* Conway, J.H., Norton, S.P., "Monstrous Moonshine", Bull. London Math. Soc. 1979

/-! ## Character Tables -/

/-- A `CharacterTable` encodes the character theory of a finite group with `n`
conjugacy classes (and hence `n` irreducible representations over ℚ).

Convention: class 0 is the identity class, irrep 0 is the trivial representation. -/
structure CharacterTable (n : ℕ) where
  /-- Size of the j-th conjugacy class -/
  classSize : Fin n → ℕ
  /-- Order of the group -/
  groupOrder : ℕ
  /-- Character value: `χ i j` = value of the i-th irreducible character
      on elements of the j-th conjugacy class -/
  χ : Fin n → Fin n → ℚ
  /-- The group order is positive -/
  groupOrder_pos : 0 < groupOrder
  /-- There is at least one conjugacy class -/
  n_pos : 0 < n
  /-- Every conjugacy class is nonempty -/
  classSize_pos : ∀ j, 0 < classSize j
  /-- The identity class (class 0) has size 1 -/
  identity_class : classSize ⟨0, n_pos⟩ = 1
  /-- The trivial character (irrep 0) takes value 1 everywhere -/
  trivial_char : ∀ j, χ ⟨0, n_pos⟩ j = 1
  /-- Class equation: ∑ |C_j| = |G| -/
  classEquation : ∑ j : Fin n, (classSize j : ℚ) = (groupOrder : ℚ)
  /-- Row orthogonality: ∑_k |C_k| χ_i(g_k) χ_j(g_k) = |G| δ_{i,j} -/
  rowOrth : ∀ i j : Fin n,
    ∑ k : Fin n, (classSize k : ℚ) * χ i k * χ j k =
      if i = j then (groupOrder : ℚ) else 0
  /-- Column orthogonality: ∑_i χ_i(g_k) χ_i(g_l) = (|G|/|C_k|) δ_{k,l} -/
  colOrth : ∀ k l : Fin n,
    ∑ i : Fin n, χ i k * χ i l =
      if k = l then (groupOrder : ℚ) / (classSize k : ℚ) else 0

namespace CharacterTable

variable {n : ℕ} (T : CharacterTable n)

    exact T.colOrth _ _;

  convert h_col_ortho using 1 ; norm_num [ T.identity_class ]

/-! ## Moonshine Data -/

/-- A `MoonshineDatum` extends a character table with a graded module structure.

    a graded vector space V = ⊕_{m ≥ 0} V_m where each V_m decomposes

  /-- Multiplicity of the i-th irrep in the m-th graded component.

namespace MoonshineDatum

variable {n : ℕ} (M : MoonshineDatum n)

/-- The McKay-Thompson coefficient: the trace of a class-j element on V_m.
    This is the m-th coefficient of the McKay-Thompson series T_{g_j}(q). -/

  ∑ i : Fin n, (M.mult i m : ℚ) * M.χ i j

/-
# Fractal Number Theory: Hausdorff and Box-Counting Dimensions of Prime Distributions

We study the set S = {1/log(p) : p prime} ⊂ ℝ, which is isometric to the primes
under the logarithmic metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|.

## Main Results

1. **dimH_logPrimeImage_eq_zero**: The Hausdorff dimension of S is 0.
2. **zero_mem_closure_logPrimeImage**: 0 is a limit point of S.
3. **logPrimeMetric_formula**: Explicit metric formula relating prime gaps to geometry.
4. **logPrimeImage_bounded**: S ⊆ (0, 1/log 2].
5. **logPrime_spacing_vanishes**: The gaps between consecutive 1/log(prime) values → 0.
6. **prime_dimension_gap**: dimH(S) = 0 yet 0 is a limit point (not isolated).

import Mathlib

open Real Set MeasureTheory Filter Topology ENNReal Nat

noncomputable section

/-! ## Core Definitions -/

/-- The logarithmic prime image: S = {1/log(p) : p is a prime natural number}. -/
def logPrimeImage : Set ℝ :=
  {x : ℝ | ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ x = 1 / Real.log p}

/-- The logarithmic prime metric on natural numbers:
d(p, q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. -/
def logPrimeMetricDist (p q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  |1 / Real.log p - 1 / Real.log q|

/-! ## Novel Definition: Box-Counting Dimension Framework

Box-counting (Minkowski) dimension for bounded subsets of ℝ.
This is distinct from Hausdorff dimension and can be positive for countable sets. -/

/-- The box-counting number N(S, ε): count of grid intervals of width ε intersecting S. -/
def boxCountingNumber (S : Set ℝ) (ε : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  if ε ≤ 0 then 0
  else (Finset.Icc (Int.floor (sInf S / ε)) (Int.ceil (sSup S / ε))).card

/-- The upper box-counting dimension:
dim_B^+(S) = limsup_{ε→0+} log(N(S,ε)) / log(1/ε). -/
def upperBoxDim (S : Set ℝ) : EReal :=
  Filter.limsup (fun ε => (Real.log (boxCountingNumber S ε : ℝ) / Real.log (1/ε) : EReal))
    (nhdsWithin (0 : ℝ) (Set.Ioi 0))

/-! ## Novel Definition: Prime Gap Energy

The prime gap energy in the logarithmic metric measures the "roughness" of
the prime distribution at a given scale exponent s. -/

/-- The prime gap energy at exponent s, summing |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|^s over
consecutive prime pairs up to bound N. This captures the fractal structure
at different scales: s=1 gives total variation, s < 1 emphasizes small gaps. -/
def primeLogGapEnergy (N : ℕ) (s : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ k ∈ Finset.range N,
    if (k.Prime ∧ (k+2).Prime) then
      |1 / Real.log (k : ℝ) - 1 / Real.log ((k+2 : ℕ) : ℝ)|^s
    else 0

/-! ## Theorem 1: Countability -/

/-- The logarithmic prime image is countable. -/
theorem logPrimeImage_countable : Set.Countable logPrimeImage :=
  Set.Countable.mono (fun x hx => by cases hx; aesop)
    (Set.countable_range (fun p : ℕ => 1 / Real.log p))

/-! ## Theorem 2: Hausdorff Dimension = 0 -/

/-- **Main Theorem**: The Hausdorff dimension of the logarithmic prime image is 0.
Every countable subset of an EMetric space has Hausdorff dimension 0.
No remetrization of a countable set can produce positive Hausdorff dimension. -/
theorem dimH_logPrimeImage_eq_zero : dimH logPrimeImage = 0 :=
  dimH_countable logPrimeImage_countable

/-! ## Theorem 3: Metric Axioms -/

/-- The logarithmic prime metric is symmetric. -/
theorem logPrimeMetric_symm (p q : ℕ) :
    logPrimeMetricDist p q = logPrimeMetricDist q p :=
  abs_sub_comm _ _

/-- The logarithmic prime metric satisfies the triangle inequality. -/

import Mathlib

/-!
# Hydrogen Atom: Dipole Transition Selection Rules

This file formalizes the electric dipole selection rules for the hydrogen atom:

- **Δm rule**: The magnetic quantum number must change by at most ±1
  for a nonzero dipole matrix element.

## Mathematical Context

The electric dipole operator for electromagnetic transitions has three
Cartesian components `x, y, z`. In spherical coordinates:
- `z = r cos θ` → involves `Y₁⁰(θ,φ)` ∝ `cos θ`
- `x = r sin θ cos φ` → involves `e^{iφ}` and `e^{-iφ}`
- `y = r sin θ sin φ` → involves `e^{iφ}` and `e^{-iφ}`

The azimuthal part of the matrix element `⟨ψ'|r̂_q|ψ⟩` contains
the integral `∫₀²π e^{-im'φ} f(φ) e^{imφ} dφ` where `f` is one of
`{1, e^{iφ}, e^{-iφ}}`. This integral vanishes unless `m' - m ∈ {0, ±1}`.

This file proves the selection rule from the orthogonality of complex
exponentials, which is the mathematical core of the selection rule.

## Key Results

* `dipole_m_selection_z`: Δm = 0 for z-polarized transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_plus`: Δm = +1 for σ⁺ transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_minus`: Δm = -1 for σ⁻ transitions
* `dipole_m_selection_vanishing`: matrix element vanishes when |Δm| > 1
-/

open scoped BigOperators

/-! ## Dipole Matrix Element (Azimuthal Part)

The azimuthal part of the dipole matrix element for the three
polarization components `q ∈ {-1, 0, +1}` is:

  I_q(m', m) = ∫₀²π e^{-im'φ} e^{iqφ} e^{imφ} dφ
             = ∫₀²π e^{i(m - m' + q)φ} dφ

This equals `2π` if `m' = m + q` and `0` otherwise.
-/

/-- The azimuthal dipole integral for polarization `q` between
magnetic quantum numbers `m` and `m'`:
  `∫₀²π exp(i(m - m' + q)φ) dφ`
This is `2π` if `m + q = m'` and `0` otherwise. -/
def azimuthalDipoleIntegral (m m' q : ℤ) : ℂ :=
  ∫ φ in (0 : ℝ)..(2 * Real.pi),
    Complex.exp (↑((m - m' + q) * φ) * Complex.I)

/-
The azimuthal dipole integral equals `2π` when `m' = m + q`.
-/
theorem azimuthalDipoleIntegral_resonant (m q : ℤ) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m (m + q) q = ↑(2 * Real.pi) := by
  unfold azimuthalDipoleIntegral;
  simp

/-
The azimuthal dipole integral vanishes when `m' ≠ m + q`.
-/
theorem azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant
    (m m' q : ℤ) (h : m' ≠ m + q) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0 := by
  convert integral_exp_mul_complex ?_ using 1;
  convert intervalIntegral.integral_congr fun x _ => ?_ using 3;
  rotate_left;
  rotate_left;
  exact ↑ ( m - m' + q ) * Complex.I;
  · exact mul_ne_zero ( Int.cast_ne_zero.mpr ( by contrapose! h; linarith ) ) Complex.I_ne_zero;
  · push_cast; ring;
  · rw [ Complex.exp_eq_one_iff.mpr ⟨ m - m' + q, by push_cast; ring ⟩ ] ; norm_num

For z-polarized light, the azimuthal integral requires `m' = m`,
i.e., Δm = 0. -/

/-
**Δm = 0 selection rule**: For z-polarized dipole transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_z (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' 0 = 0 := by
  grind +suggestions

/-! ## Selection Rule for Circular Polarizations (q = ±1)

For right/left circularly polarized light, the azimuthal integral
requires `m' = m ± 1`, i.e., Δm = ±1. -/

/-
**Δm = +1 selection rule**: For σ⁺ transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m + 1`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_plus (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m + 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' 1 = 0 := by
  exact?

/-
**Δm = -1 selection rule**: For σ⁻ transitions,
the azimuthal integral vanishes unless `m' = m - 1`.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_minus (m m' : ℤ) (hne : m' ≠ m - 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' (-1) = 0 := by
  convert azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' ( -1 ) _ using 1;
  exact hne

/-! ## Combined Selection Rule -/

/-- **Full Δm selection rule**: The azimuthal dipole integral for
any spherical polarization component `q ∈ {-1, 0, 1}` vanishes
unless `m' = m + q`. This is the fundamental selection rule for
the magnetic quantum number. -/
theorem dipole_m_selection_general (m m' q : ℤ) (h : m' ≠ m + q) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0 :=
  azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' q h

/-- **Contrapositive form of the selection rule**: If the azimuthal
dipole matrix element is nonzero, then the change in `m` must be
exactly `q`, i.e., `Δm = q ∈ {-1, 0, +1}`. -/
theorem dipole_m_selection_contrapositive (m m' q : ℤ)
    (hne : azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q ≠ 0) :
    m' = m + q := by
  by_contra h
  exact hne (azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant m m' q h)

/-
**Vanishing for forbidden transitions**: If `m' - m ∉ {-1, 0, 1}`,
then the azimuthal dipole integral vanishes for ALL polarization
components. This is the strong form of the selection rule.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_vanishing (m m' : ℤ)
    (hforbidden : ¬(m' - m = 0 ∨ m' - m = 1 ∨ m' - m = -1)) :
    (∀ q ∈ ({-1, 0, 1} : Set ℤ), azimuthalDipoleIntegral m m' q = 0) := by
  -- Apply the off_resonant theorem to each case.
  intro q hq
  apply azimuthalDipoleIntegral_off_resonant;
  grind

/-! ## Selection Rule Completeness -/

/-
The allowed transitions are exactly those with `Δm ∈ {-1, 0, 1}`:
for each such value there exists a nonzero matrix element.
-/
theorem dipole_m_selection_complete (m : ℤ) (q : ℤ) (hq : q = -1 ∨ q = 0 ∨ q = 1) :
    azimuthalDipoleIntegral m (m + q) q ≠ 0 := by
  exact azimuthalDipoleIntegral_resonant m q ▸ by norm_num [ Real.pi_ne_zero ] ;

end

For an *abelian* anyon theory whose anyon labels form a finite abelian group `A` with

3. **A fully worked example.** For the cyclic anyon model `A = ZMod n` we *construct*

   conditional unitarity theorem into an unconditional statement and exhibiting the
   discrete Fourier matrix `S_{a,b} = (1/√n) exp(2πi a b / n)`.

open Finset

namespace TopologicalOrderGenus

/-! ## Section 1: Ground-State Degeneracy on Genus-`g` Surfaces

For an abelian theory the genus-`g` ground space is `A^{⊗g}`, so its dimension is
`|A|^g`.  We package this as `GSD` and prove its structural laws. -/

/-- Ground-state degeneracy of an abelian anyon theory `A` on a genus-`g` surface. -/
def GSD (A : Type*) [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : ℕ := Fintype.card A ^ g

variable {A : Type*}

-- !-- `GSD A g = d ^ g` by definition; the closed-form degeneracy law. -- !--
/-- **Closed form.** The genus-`g` degeneracy equals `d ^ g` with `d = |A|`. -/
theorem GSD_eq_pow [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : GSD A g = Fintype.card A ^ g := rfl

-- !-- Each added handle multiplies the degeneracy by `d = |A|`; this is `pow_succ`. -- !--
/-- **Per-handle recursion.** Adding one handle multiplies degeneracy by `d`. -/
theorem GSD_handle [Fintype A] (g : ℕ) : GSD A (g + 1) = Fintype.card A * GSD A g := by
  rw [GSD, GSD, pow_succ, mul_comm]

-- !-- Genus is additive under connected sum, so degeneracy is multiplicative (`pow_add`). -- !--
/-- **Connected-sum multiplicativity.** `Σ_g # Σ_h` has degeneracy
    `GSD A g · GSD A h` since genus adds under connected sum. -/
theorem GSD_connected_sum [Fintype A] (g h : ℕ) :

  rw [GSD, GSD, GSD, pow_add]

/-- **Torus.** On the torus the degeneracy is the number of anyon types. -/
theorem GSD_torus [Fintype A] : GSD A 1 = Fintype.card A := by

/-- **Combinatorial model.** `GSD A g` counts the configurations `Fin g → A`. -/

  rw [GSD, Fintype.card_pi_const]

/-! ## Section 2: Modular Braiding and the Unitary S-matrix

A nondegenerate braiding on an abelian theory is a self-pairing of `A` by additive

/-- A **modular braiding** on a finite abelian group `A`: a family of additive
    characters `χ_a` depending homomorphically on `a` (`χ_{a+a'} = χ_a · χ_{a'}`) and
    *nondegenerate* (only `a = 0` gives the trivial character).  This is the abelian
    anyon braiding bicharacter `(a,b) ↦ χ_a(b)`. -/

  /-- The braiding character of anyon `a`. -/
  chi : A → AddChar A ℂ
  /-- The braiding is bilinear: `χ_{a+a'} = χ_a · χ_{a'}`. -/
  map_add' : ∀ a a', chi (a + a') = chi a * chi a'

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A] [Fintype A] (M : ModularBraiding A)

-- !-- `χ_0 = χ_0 · χ_0` forces `χ_0 = 1`, the trivial character. -- !--
/-- The vacuum braids trivially: `χ_0` is the trivial character. -/
lemma map_zero : M.chi 0 = 0 := by

/-- Nondegeneracy makes the assignment `a ↦ χ_a` injective. -/

lemma chi_diff_eq_zero_iff (a b : A) : M.chi a * (M.chi b)⁻¹ = 0 ↔ a = b := by
